(1)     Patrick Schaefer and Keven Gedko, co-presiding hearing examiners, respectfully

submit this Certification of Stipulation to the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission

(“Commission”) in accordance with 1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC. This Certification concerns the

contested Comprehensive Stipulation (“Stipulation”) filed on June 22, 2026. Having reviewed

the Stipulation as well as the full record of this proceeding, the Hearing Examiners certify it

to the Commission with a recommendation that it be approved with modifications.



I.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

(2)     The Stipulation presented to the Commission seeks to balance Southwestern Public Service

Company’s (“SPS”) need to recover the reasonable costs of an evolving electric system with the

Commission’s responsibility to ensure that those costs, and the benefits associated with them, are

fairly reflected in New Mexico retail rates. SPS’s changing generation portfolio, substantial capital

investments, and evolving customer demand present important questions concerning revenue

requirements, cost allocation, and the treatment of federal tax incentives.

(3)     In this context, SPS sought in its initial Application an increase of approximately $175.4

million in annual retail base-rate revenues, which was reduced through filed corrections to a

request of approximately $167.5 million. The Stipulation, filed by SPS and nine intervenor-

signatories on June 22, 2026, provides instead for a $90 million increase, effective December 1,

2026. Commission Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) opposed several provisions of the Stipulation,

and the Stipulation as a whole, while the New Mexico Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources

Department took no position.

(4)     The Hearing Examiners recommend approval of the principal financial terms of the

Stipulation, including the 9.5% return on equity, 7.59% weighted average cost of capital, capital

structure consisting of 54.7% equity and 45.3% debt, and zero cash working capital. They also

conclude that Staff’s objections concerning SPS’s future test year, forecasted jurisdictional

allocators, and linkage-data requirements do not warrant rejection of the negotiated revenue

increase. In particular, differences between New Mexico and Texas ratemaking methodologies do

not, standing alone, establish that SPS’s New Mexico rates are unreasonable. The recommended

approval of the $90 million increase remains subject to the specific adjustments addressed in this

Certification.

(5)     The equitable allocation of costs and benefits is a central consideration in the Hearing

Examiners’ recommended modifications. Under Sections 1.3 and 1.17, they recommend that New

Mexico customers receive the full accredited-capacity benefit of the directly assigned Cunningham

battery energy storage system, without the stipulated reduction for the seasonal planning reserve

margin. Under Section 1.11, they recommend retaining the four-coincident-peak methodology for

calculating the system load factor, and allocating production tax credits among customer classes

using      the     average-and-excess-demand      four-coincident-peak     methodology.      These

recommendations seek to maintain a reasonable relationship between the costs assigned to

customers and the benefits they receive, while preserving the opportunity to evaluate alternative

allocation methodologies through previously approved stakeholder workshops.

(6)     Particularly significant in this proceeding is the determination of the ratemaking treatment

of federal production tax credits (“PTCs”) and investment tax credits (“ITCs”) associated with

SPS’s renewable generation and battery storage facilities. Important aspects of that treatment had

previously been reserved from prior cases for consideration in a general rate case. The Stipulation

now provides a framework for determining when and how those benefits are credited to customers,

how the costs of monetizing the credits are recovered, and how outstanding balances are treated

recovered through the fuel and purchased power cost adjustment clause, subject to a maximum

carrying period of 365 days and an earlier end to accrual when monetization occurs or reasonably

could have occurred. They also recommend approval of the stipulated five-year amortization of

ITC benefits, limitations on transfer costs, and treatment of eligible unamortized balances, with a

modification to Section 1.8(B)(d) to make the applicable rate of return mandatory for both SPS

and customers. These determinations establish important aspects of the financial treatment of

federal tax incentives while preserving Commission review of matters expressly reserved for

future proceedings.

(7)     The Hearing Examiners also recommend targeted adjustments to ensure that costs

recovered from customers are adequately supported by the record. These include limiting recovery

of rate-case and other regulatory expenses to $3,338,676, amortized over three years, and

disallowing unsupported annual Community Solar Portal operating expenses. They recommend

approval of the clarified excess-liability-insurance regulatory-asset balance of $26,233,655,

amortized over three years. The remaining provisions of the Stipulation address depreciation and

generation-unit service-life extensions, recovery of regulatory assets, capacity requirements, the

Electric Affordability Program, and various tariff and rate-design matters. The Hearing Examiners

generally recommend approval of these provisions, subject to the qualifications and limitations

addressed in this Certification.

(8)     Considered as a whole, the Stipulation reflects a negotiated accommodation of competing

interests arising from SPS’s substantial capital investments, changing generation resources, and

evolving customer demand. It substantially reduces SPS’s requested rate increase while

III.    DISCUSSION

A.      Legal Standards

(20)    Three fundamental legal standards govern review of the proposed Stipulation, the Public

Utility Act14 (“PUA”) and applicable ratemaking rules, including the requirements for a future test

year,15 the Commission’s rules16 and the three-part test governing approval of stipulations,17

particularly contested settlements, and the evidentiary burden on a utility seeking a rate increase.18



        1. Public Utility Rates

(21)    The PUA grants the Commission “general and exclusive power and jurisdiction to regulate

and supervise every public utility in respect to its rates and service regulations . . . and to do all

things necessary and convenient in the exercise of its power and jurisdiction.”19 The PUA requires

that “[e]very rate made, demanded or received by any public utility shall be just and reasonable.”20

The New Mexico Supreme Court in Coalition for Clean Affordable Energy v. New Mexico Public

Regulation Commission found that to satisfy the just and reasonable standard rates must be “neither

unreasonably high so as to unjustly burden ratepayers with excessive rates nor unreasonably low

(22)    Relatedly, neither the PUA nor New Mexico case law confines the Commission to one

ratemaking formula or one analytical method when setting or approving rates. The legislature has

allowed the Commission great flexibility in the methods to be used in achieving those goals.23 The

New Mexico Supreme Court has ruled that “[t]he touchstone is the reasonableness of the ultimate

decision.”24 The Certification of Stipulation in Docket No. No. 19-00170-UT expressed this

flexibility and discretion, stating that “[u]nder the statutory standard of just and reasonable it is the

result reached, not the method employed, which is controlling. It is not the theory but the impact

of the rate which counts.”25 Even a defect or disagreement in a particular intermediate

methodology is not necessarily dispositive if the ultimate rate order is independently supported

and just and reasonable. This principle supplies the doctrinal basis for some negotiated “black box”

outcomes.26

the New Mexico Supreme Court has stated, New Mexico’s PUA “expresses a clear intent to

displace competition with regulation in the area of utility service.”27 Ratemaking is therefore not

(24)      Additionally, Section 62-6-14(D) NMSA 1978 requires the Commission to establish rates

based on the test period that best reflects the conditions expected when those rates take effect,

giving due consideration to whether a proposed future test period best reflects those conditions.

The Commission’s Future Test Year (“FTY”) rule, 17.1.3 NMAC, permits utilities to develop FTY

estimates using adjustments, forecasts, budgets, or other reasonable methods, provided that those

estimates are fully explained, justified, and supported by verifiable linkage data connecting the

historical base period to the future test year.28 This rule further requires that material changes in

cost drivers be separately identified and justified, that projections be traceable to historical data or

supported by an understandable alternative basis, and that forecast assumptions and changes in

activity levels be quantified and adequately supported.29 Finally, 17.1.3.19 NMAC establishes

procedures for revisions to the original application, including notice and explanation of material

changes and documentation of other revisions to preserve their verifiability.

        2. Commission Approval of Stipulations


(25)    The Commission has a long-standing policy to encourage stipulations. This encouragement

extends even to those which are, in whole or part, “black box” settlements, i.e., settlements where

all or some of the components may be unspecified, but the signatories agree on the result.30

Notwithstanding this encouragement, settlements and stipulations, the Signatories must support

the proposed Stipulation with sufficient evidence and legal argument demonstrating to the

Commission that the resulting rates in the stipulation are fair, just, reasonable, and in the public

interest.31 The Certification of Stipulation in Docket No. 22-00286-UT articulates the principle as

follows:

        while the stipulation indicates that the parties (and not necessarily all of them) have
        reached agreement that a particular resolution meets some legal standard and is
        maximally desirable as a matter of policy…[the] Commission must be persuaded
        that this is so, and it is free to reject the parties’ views on the subject.32

(26)    In the review of stipulations, the Commission applies the provisions of 1.2.2.20 NMAC

and must first establish whether the stipulation is uncontested or contested. In the present case,

where the stipulation is contested, 1.2.2.20(B) NMAC applies. That rule provides for a range of

procedural requirements, such as establishing filing and service requirements,33 a reconciliation

Discussion and Determination

(286)   Section 1.8(A) addresses the interval between crediting customers with the value of Solar

Project PTCs and SPS’s use or transfer of those credits. During that interval, the DTA reflects value

already provided to customers but not yet realized by SPS. The dispute is principally over the

measure of compensation for that balance. SPS initially requested a rate of return to be equivalent

to the 8.21% WACC proposed in the original Application while the Stipulation adopts the 5.29%

cost of long-term debt. At the same time, Staff recommends its lower weighted cost of debt, stated

as 2.33% in testimony opposing the Stipulation.

(287)   The distinction between the debt measures matters. The stipulated 5.29% is a direct long-

term borrowing-cost benchmark; the weighted cost of debt reflects that rate multiplied by the debt

share of the capital structure—approximately 2.40% at the stipulated 45.3% debt ratio. The DTA,

however, is neither a discrete loan nor an investment in utility plant. The long-term-debt rate

reasonably approximates the cost of financing the outstanding balance without including the equity

return that formed part of SPS’s original WACC request. Staff’s concern that a higher carrying

charge could reduce the incentive to monetize PTCs promptly deserves consideration, but a

definite limit on the period of accrual addresses that concern more directly than requiring the

weighted cost of debt.

(288)   The stipulated recovery mechanism likewise follows the character of the balance. Both

PTC benefits and the associated DTA change as credits are generated, utilized, or transferred.

Recovering the carrying charge through the FPPCAC, rather than through a future-test-year

estimate in base rates, more closely aligns the charge with the outstanding amount and with the

PTC benefits credited through that mechanism. The Stipulation also removes $5,770,468 in New
